candidateRows: Human limitations constrain descriptions of God, who is best understood as the source of existence, a relational presence, and the ground of purposeful life.
This establishes the theistic side's governing conception of God and explains why divine reality cannot be exhaustively captured by ordinary human definitions.
In response to the opening question about what God is, Wolpe frames the debate through human cognitive limitation and supplies a deliberately restrained definition of God.
God is a human and fear-driven invention that supplies parental consolation, moral authority, and in its worst form a demand for totalitarian submission.
This directly states the atheist critique at the center of the motion by explaining religious belief as projection and connecting it to authoritarian social consequences.
Hitchens answers the opening definition of God by tracing gods from human invention and psychological need through polytheism and monotheism toward zero.
Explaining religious belief through believers' psychological needs does not disprove it, because an alleged motive for belief is separate from whether the belief is true.
This challenges the validity of Hitchens's projection argument and protects the rational standing of theistic belief from dismissal through motive attribution alone.
Hitchens's claim that belief in God arises from fear, weakness, a desire for love, and a wish for authority.
Wolpe argues that religious belief is being assigned a psychological cause while atheism is treated as logical, and insists that truth requires direct argument rather than motive attribution.
A possible first cause is categorically different from a supervising religious deity, and natural explanations remove the need to assume either kind of divine mover.
The move separates minimal deism from revealed religion and argues that neither cosmic order nor biological life requires a divine explanatory assumption.
Wolpe's objection that psychological explanations do not address whether belief in God is actually true.
Hitchens concedes that his earlier account was incomplete, distinguishes an impersonal creator from an intervening religious God, and argues that nature works without either assumption.
Consciousness, love, meaning, and the existence of anything at all indicate that intangible reality may be fundamental and make belief in God reasonable.
This supplies the principal positive case for theism by combining lived awareness of immaterial value with features of existence that Wolpe regards as suggestive of transcendence.
Hitchens's contention that natural and scientific accounts work without any hypothesis of a creator or divine mover.
Wolpe rejects laboratory proof as the proper model for God, appeals to consciousness and meaning, and then identifies existence and scientific mystery as signs of something greater.
Modern cosmology and evolution provide verifiable, majestic natural accounts of existence, while their waste and extinction make a providential religious plan implausible.
The argument directly counters transcendental inference from wonder by offering testable natural explanations and using pervasive destruction against claims of purposeful divine design.
Wolpe's argument that existence, consciousness, love, and scientific mystery suggest a reality greater than the material world.
Hitchens invokes cosmology, stellar destruction, common material origins, human evolution, and mass extinction to contrast scientific grandeur with unverifiable creation stories.
Material causes cannot account for directed human choice, because genetics and environment are given conditions, so free will requires an immaterial dimension grounded in God.
This turns human freedom into a central argument for theism and challenges materialism to explain agency without reducing choices to predetermined physical conditions.
Hitchens's materialist account of human beings and his claim that cosmic and biological history require no divine explanation.
Wolpe disputes the historical characterization of religion and then argues that materialism leaves every action fixed by initial conditions unless persons possess something immaterial.
Evolutionary and genetic processes contain genuine contingency rather than predetermination, and their explanatory and practical success surpasses scriptural claims of personal divine authorship.
This directly attacks the premise of Wolpe's free-will argument by denying biological determinism and presenting empirical naturalism as richer and more useful than revelation.
Wolpe's claim that materialism makes all human action predetermined and therefore cannot account for free will without God.
Hitchens uses evolutionary contingency and random mutation to deny predetermination, then points to genetic medicine and verifiability as advantages over scriptural explanation.
Growing scientific knowledge strengthens the case for skepticism rather than faith, while interventionist religion converts unverifiable metaphysics into coercive claims of salvation and punishment.
This joins the epistemic and political halves of the atheist case by defending doubt as the proper response to ignorance and rejecting religion's claimed total authority.
Wolpe's claim that religious conviction resembles knowledge of love or beauty and makes sense of mysteries outside empirical science.

Hitchens argues that science has displaced religious explanations while revealing deeper ignorance, making inquiry essential, and warns that religious metaphysics carries public demands and sanctions.
Judaism centrally prescribes evolving forms of goodness, and religious faith demonstrably gives people meaning while motivating charity, civic participation, and aid to others.
This answers the charge that religion is inherently totalitarian and useless by presenting moral development and observable prosocial conduct as central fruits of faith.
Hitchens's portrayal of religion as coercive, totalizing, epistemically useless, and largely irrelevant to humanity's real dilemmas.
Wolpe distinguishes evolving Judaism from inherently authoritarian religion and cites believers' reported meaning, generosity, volunteering, voting, and international aid as beneficial effects.
Religious charity frequently combines material assistance with proselytism, false explanations, and exploitation of vulnerable recipients.
The move directly contests the claim that religion’s charitable activity demonstrates its moral value or beneficial effects.
Wolpe’s preceding claim that faith motivates extensive charitable work and overwhelmingly produces goodness.
After allowing private consolation, Hitchens challenges public religious privilege and argues that charitable activity cannot substitute for evidence or excuse proselytism.
Judaism centrally directs people toward justice, character refinement, and decent treatment despite abuses committed by religious authorities.
The move supplies Wolpe’s principal textual and traditional basis for treating religion as a system oriented toward goodness.
Hitchens’s claim that religious charity evades evidential questions and can become coercive or deceptive proselytism.
Wolpe invokes biblical justice and the broader Jewish interpretive tradition, concedes that authority can be abused, and disputes treating only religious harms as representative.
Religion itself is objectionable because its foundational laws encode tribal exclusion, violence, slavery, patriarchy, and other human prejudices.
This is a direct defense of the atheist motion-level thesis that religion is a human construction whose own doctrines cause harm.
Wolpe’s accusation that Hitchens discounts religious good while treating every religious wrong as representative of religion.
Hitchens distinguishes his position from merely blaming religious institutions and argues that the content and social assumptions of scripture reveal its primitive human origins.
Religious traditions are humanly transmitted and historically evolving systems capable of refining themselves and discarding inherited moral defects.
The move answers the foundational-text critique by making moral development within tradition essential to Wolpe’s defense of religion.
Hitchens’s argument that biblical commands display primitive tribal morality and therefore expose religion as man-made.
Wolpe accepts human participation in composing scripture but argues that religions, like societies and ideologies, evolve and progressively remove harmful inherited elements.
Faith confers no unique moral capacity because an unbeliever can perform every genuinely moral action available to a believer.
The challenge attacks the necessity of religion for goodness and establishes a central comparative test between belief and unbelief.
Wolpe’s contention that evolving religious systems can refine character, discard harmful teachings, and make people better.
Hitchens argues that prohibitions on familiar wrongs do not establish religious distinctiveness and asks for a good act unavailable to nonbelievers.
Religion uniquely motivates practices and experiences of sanctity whose moral and emotional meaning cannot be reproduced by disbelief alone.
The move supplies Wolpe’s principal answer to the claim that faith adds nothing distinctive to moral or meaningful human conduct.
Hitchens’s challenge to identify a good moral statement or action that a person without faith could not perform.
Wolpe concedes shared physical capacity but distinguishes actual religious motivation and a sanctified relationship, illustrating the point through a family ritual.
Honest acceptance of mortality and suffering is preferable to religious consolation, while philosophy and literature offer richer ethical resources without illusion.
The move directly advances the atheist alternative to religious consolation, moral instruction, and promised relief from despair.
The contention that without religious teaching society lacks moral structure and people in despair lack meaningful support.
Hitchens presents mortality, entropy, grief, and struggle as realities to face without invented reassurance and characterizes false consolation as disrespectful and ineffective.
Religious community and belief in meaning provide profound, nontrivial consolation amid death and grief, even when that meaning cannot be empirically proved.
This move gives the central theistic defense of faith as meaningful consolation rather than cheap evasion or harmful illusion.
Hitchens’s argument that accepting despair and mortality without illusion is more honest and humane than religious consolation.
Drawing on encounters with bereaved families, Wolpe argues that community, prayer, and belief in a meaningful world meet deep human needs under extreme anguish.
Religion is not the primary cause of war; material conflict and ordinary human aggression better explain violence, while religion attempts moral restraint.
The move directly contests the motion-level allegation that religious belief uniquely or predominantly generates organized violence.
The broader atheist position that religion and divinely grounded authority are intrinsic sources of cruelty, coercion, and violence.
Wolpe attributes most ostensibly religious wars to land, power, and resources, invokes secular regimes, and locates aggression in imperfect human nature.
Religion intensifies ordinary tribal conflict by supplying divine mandates, making it a powerful multiplier of violence and political intransigence.
This is the principal atheist answer on violence, connecting supernatural authority to escalated conflict across several major historical cases.
Wolpe’s claim that wars arise mainly from material interests and human aggression rather than religion itself.
Hitchens concedes natural human aggression but argues that heavenly authorization magnifies it, citing tribal conquest, Rwanda, territorial disputes, and Nazi religious language.
Religious belief is not a scientific assertion, and humanity's recurrent discovery of God supports the possibility of a natural or revealed awareness of God.
The answer directly addresses whether belief in God requires scientific proof or prior human instruction, a central epistemological issue in the motion.
The audience question suggesting that God would not be independently inferred without prior written or oral religious instruction.

After a question separates God's existence from religion and asks whether Wolpe would discover God without instruction, Wolpe distinguishes religious from scientific criteria and answers affirmatively.
Science can coexist with private religious belief, but scientific accomplishment does not validate religion, and many ultimate questions may remain undecidable.
The move defines the atheist position on scientific uncertainty and rejects the inference that prominent religious scientists provide epistemic support for faith.
Wolpe's appeal to prominent believing scientists and his question about whether Hitchens expects science eventually to solve everything.
Hitchens accepts enduring scientific uncertainty, then uses examples of scientists with implausible extra-scientific beliefs to separate scientific competence from religious justification.
Shared moral rules arise across societies but remain context-sensitive, while supposed divine absolutes contain contradictions and evade the necessary work of ethical reasoning.
This directly advances the debate's central dispute over whether moral meaning requires divine authority or can instead emerge through human ethical reflection.
The audience request that Hitchens identify whether universal morality exists and, if it does, explain where it originates.
Answering a two-part audience question, Hitchens treats the widely recurring reciprocal rule as the nearest moral universal while arguing that rigid scriptural formulations fail in difficult cases.
God grounds real moral right and wrong without eliminating moral reasoning, whereas a purely material account of evolved primates reduces morality to interests and power.
The proposition supplies Wolpe's core case that objective moral meaning depends on a transcendent dimension while preserving questioning and reasoning within religious tradition.
Hitchens's argument that divine moral absolutes are contradictory devices for avoiding independent ethical thought.

Wolpe denies that Jewish commandments mechanically settle every case, emphasizes reasoning within Judaism, and argues that objective morality requires more than evolved biology and competing interests.
Positing a creator to explain cosmic origins merely creates an infinite regress, and even an uncaused first cause would not establish a personal, interventionist God.
The move directly attacks a principal argument for God's existence and separates an unexplained cosmic cause from the specific deity asserted by religion.
The audience argument that the existence of a universe, space-time structure, and human life makes more sense if grounded in God.

Asked why anything exists rather than nothing, Hitchens refers to naturalistic cosmology, argues that adding a creator does not solve the explanatory problem, and limits what a first cause could prove.
Human experiences of transcendence, ecstasy, beauty, love, and mortality are real and important but provide no warrant for a supernatural realm.
The argument counters the claim that profound meaning or numinous experience supports faith by offering a fully naturalistic interpretation of those experiences.
The suggestion that Hitchens's own sensitivity to meaning or transcendence may reveal an implicit religious belief.
Hitchens acknowledges a universal human need for transcendent and ecstatic experience, connects it to beauty and awareness of impermanence, and denies that it discloses anything supernatural.
All religions wrongly privilege faith over reason, while Islam's claim to final revelation and its political program make its current form especially prone to intolerance and violence.
The move states Hitchens's general epistemic objection to religion and connects exclusive revelation claims to concrete political and coercive consequences.
The Sufi audience member's objection that Hitchens's book title specifically negates a central Islamic profession and unfairly targets Islam.

Hitchens explains that religions share an epistemic defect but vary historically in danger, then argues that final-revelation claims, religious law, and holy war make contemporary Islam especially harmful.
Nonbelievers can feel compelling reasons to behave morally, but only a transcendent moral order makes goodness universally binding regardless of preference, circumstance, or observation.
This clarification preserves Wolpe's central moral argument while answering the apparent concession that an atheist can possess sincere reasons for moral conduct.
The questioner's claim that Wolpe inconsistently denies atheistic moral reasons while acknowledging Hitchens's sincere commitment to justice and goodness.

Wolpe distinguishes personal motivation from the foundation of moral obligation, arguing that humanly created standards are defeasible while goodness grounded beyond humanity remains universally true.
Religious institutions cannot credibly claim to ground morality when secular law must restrain their abuses and secular constitutional authority must discipline prophetic power.
The argument directly rebuts the claim that transcendent authority protects against moral relativism by showing secular institutions correcting conduct defended or concealed by religion.
Wolpe's claim that morality woven into a transcendent order is more stable and universally binding than standards created solely by human beings.
Hitchens invokes clerical abuse and religious deference to institutional authority, then argues that legal and constitutional constraints are what make religious actors publicly accountable.
God's freedom does not generate the same regress as human freedom because God is eternal and nonbiological, while randomness cannot explain intentional human choice.
The response defends the debate's theistic account of human freedom against both an infinite-regress objection and an attempted deterministic model based on pseudorandom outputs.
The audience challenge that a deity's free will either requires another giver, creates infinite regress, or should be reproducible by deterministic randomness.

Wolpe rejects an analogy between an eternal deity and biological humans, then argues that producing unpredictable numbers remains categorically different from an agent intentionally choosing among actions.
